name: The Phantom kit
change: The first cut of the style, taken from Persona 5: red, black and white only, every panel cut on a slant, cut-out ransom letters for the logo, a turning sunburst and halftone dots behind everything. Six core screens: Title, Main menu, Battle command, Event, Pause and Settings.

q.x: It is loud already, but flat: panels sit on the page and nothing overlaps or moves much yet. Battle is still a normal Pokémon layout with slanted boxes.
q.b: First pass, so there is nothing to beat. It sets the rules every later pass has to top.
q.p: Yes. Battle only has the command list; moves, party, bag and targets each need a page. That is pass 2.
q.m: Pause is one list with the party beside it, and Settings is one page with six tabs. Both work but both are crowded; they get split up in pass 4.
q.k: Only because of the sprites. Types and Poké Balls are tiny; later passes have to pull Pokémon things into the style itself.

name: Battle leaves the box
change: Battle stops being a Pokémon layout with slanted boxes. Commands burst out of your Pokémon in a jagged star, each on its own key, the way Persona 5 puts orders around the hero. Your party stands in a stack down the right edge with live HP. Black slanted bars frame the field like a film shot. Fight, Pokémon and Bag each open their own page, and a hit gets a full-screen splash.

q.x: Much more. The command burst and the Super Effective splash are the first things on the page that could not be mistaken for any other Pokémon game.
q.b: Pass 1 had four words in a column. Now each command has a key, a size and an angle, the party is always in view, and moves show their type, power, PP and how well they hit before you choose.
q.p: Four added. Moves, party and bag used to be nowhere; they are full pages now so the battle screen holds only the fight.
q.m: Not touched this pass. In battle, X on the burst is Run and Info opens foe details; Pause still needs its own pass.
q.k: Better: type colours carry the move cards, HP bars keep green, yellow and red, Poké Balls count the foe's team, and the run's real limits (10 heals, 6 revives) sit on the Bag page.

name: The run gets a calendar
change: Outside battle, every screen now carries a stage stamp in the top corner, built like Persona 5's date: a huge stage number, the region on a red tag and the time and weather in marker pen. The route is a subway-style map of diamond stops over the region's town map. Events are split in two: the character leans in from the side and talks, and only after you press does the choice page appear, with what each choice costs. Rewards are dealt as three cards. The Mart has a clerk, a wallet and a running cart total.

q.x: Yes. Big character art leaning into frame, dealt cards and the outlined stage number give each page one loud thing to look at.
q.b: Pass 2 only fixed battle. This pass covers the other half of a run, and the old one-page event (text and choices on top of each other) is replaced by talk then choice.
q.p: Four added. Splitting talk from choice also follows the rule that text stays until you press and rewards only come after.
q.m: Esc on the map opens the menu and C jumps straight to the party. The menu itself is still the pass 1 list; it is the next pass.
q.k: More than before: the route sits on the real region map, stops use Poké Balls, the Mart clerk is the game's own sprite, and the stage stamp shows time and weather, which matter for evolutions.

name: Menus get rooms
change: The pause list becomes a hub: your trainer stands huge on the right, the chosen word swells to twice the size, and each word opens its own page. New pages for the Pokémon summary (with a six-point stat web, the Pokémon answer to Persona's stat star), the Pokédex, a Trainer card laid out like a calling card, and Save slots. Settings stops being one crowded page: a hub of six big tiles, then one short page each, never more than six rows.

q.x: Yes. The trainer filling the pause screen and the stat web give the menus the big-art feel the battle already had.
q.b: Pass 1 squeezed seven jobs and the whole party onto one pause page and all settings behind six tiny tabs. Every job now has room, and Settings rows are big enough to read from the couch.
q.p: Eleven added. Settings alone went from one page to seven.
q.m: This pass is the answer: Esc opens the hub anywhere outside battle, Settings is the sixth word, and Q/E flips between its pages without going back.
q.k: The summary keeps what players expect (types, ability, nature, held item, four moves, Exp bar); the Pokédex shows dark shapes for unseen Pokémon and the game's Mastery ranks.

name: Everything moves into everything
change: Motion pass. Changing page is now a morph: the header, the stage stamp, your trainer, your Pokémon, the party strip and the key hints each slide and resize from where they were to where they belong on the next page, while a red, black and white blade wipes the rest. Idle screens loop without a seam: the chosen item jitters, trainers breathe, the dots drift. Three new battle moments: a Mega Evolution cut-in across the eyes, a win splash with a line from your trainer, and a result tally where Exp bars fill and numbers punch in.

q.x: This is the pass that makes it feel like Persona rather than look like it. The cut-in and the win splash are the showiest pages so far.
q.b: Passes 1 to 4 were still pictures with slide-ins. Now nothing just appears: each page grows out of the one before, and each loop returns to its first frame.
q.p: Three added. Win and Result are separate on purpose, so the splash stays clean and the numbers get room.
q.m: Opening Pause, picking a word and landing on its page is one unbroken move; the trainer shrinks from the hub into the Trainer card. Settings pages slide along the rail the same way.
q.k: Mega Evolution uses the game's own Mega ring and stone art, Exp bars fill the way they always have, and Red's victory line is six dots, because Red never talks.

name: Blue version: Midnight
change: The style stops being one skin. Pokémon games come as versions, and so do Persona games, so each trainer now gets a version that borrows a different Persona. First is Blue version, taken from Persona 3 Reload: deep water blue, cyan light and glow instead of red and black, one clean slant instead of jagged cuts, bubbles rising where the dots were, a moon beside the stage stamp. The battle command star becomes a ring with a turning dashed rim. Blue stands where Red stood on every screen, with his own win line. Use the Version buttons above the stage to switch; all 27 screens have both.

q.x: It is calmer than Phantom on purpose, but the glow, the moon and the water give it its own kind of show. Having two looks at all is the big jump.
q.b: Passes 1 to 5 were one look with no way to tell runs apart. Now the look itself says whose run it is. Colours were also pulled out into named tokens, which is what makes versions possible.
q.p: No new pages this pass; every existing page gained a second look. A Version select page comes in pass 9.
q.m: Same pages, same keys. Settings › Look will get a Version row in pass 9.
q.k: More than any pass so far: Red and Blue versions are the oldest Pokémon idea there is, and the rival finally has his own look.

name: Yellow version: Channel
change: The third version, taken from Persona 4 Golden. Where Phantom cuts and Midnight glows, Channel is a TV set: bright yellow with moving colour bars and scan lines, every panel rounded with a thick black outline and a drop shadow, chunky friendly lettering, a spinning sun as the weather forecast beside the stage stamp, and the battle command star turned into a rounded TV screen. Hilda is the trainer. All 27 screens.

q.x: It is the loudest of the three and the most cheerful. The colour bars and the thick outlines read from across a room.
q.b: Pass 6 proved a second version could work by changing colour and glow. This one changes shape as well: slanted cut panels become rounded outlined ones, which the token work in pass 6 did not cover, so accent text got its own token too.
q.p: No new pages; every page gained a third look.
q.m: Unchanged. The Settings rows turn into rounded switches and sliders here, which suits them better than slants did.
q.k: Yes. Yellow version was the Pikachu one, and this is the look where the sprites feel most at home: bright, toy-like, sunny.

name: Green version: Fantasia
change: The fourth version, taken from Metaphor: ReFantazio. Nothing here is flat colour: backgrounds are grainy verdigris paint, the black shapes have torn, brushed edges, and thin gilt lines frame every panel. Lettering is a tall serif with a gold drop capital and italics. The slant is gone; everything sits upright and is built on circles: an astrolabe turns behind the pages, map stops are ringed medals, and the battle commands sit around a turning wheel instead of a star. Green is the trainer. All 27 screens.

q.x: In a different way from the others: rich instead of loud. The turning gilt rings, the paint grain and the serif capitals make it look like a storybook.
q.b: Midnight and Channel changed colour and panel shape. Fantasia changes the material (paint and paper instead of flat ink), the lettering and the geometry, and moves the six battle commands onto a wheel.
q.p: No new pages; every page gained a fourth look.
q.m: Unchanged in structure. The pause words stand upright with diamond bullets, and Settings rows read like a ledger with gilt rules.
q.k: Green version was the very first Pokémon game in Japan, so it suits the old-book look. Types sit on small heraldic ribbons and HP bars keep their colours inside gilt frames.

name: Pick your version
change: The four looks stop being a hidden switch and become a choice the player makes. A new Version Select page lines the trainers up in five slanted columns, each drawn in its own style, and the one you pick opens wide. A fifth version arrives, Gold, in the style of the Velvet Room: blue curtains, gold trim, arched windows, and titles dealt out as playing cards. Settings › Look now names your version, the title screen wears a version tag, and switching plays a full-screen flash with the version's name.

q.x: Yes. The select page shows all five styles side by side at once, which no earlier pass could, and the Gold version adds a rich, quiet look to contrast the loud ones.
q.b: Passes 6 to 8 added looks you could only reach from the viewer. Now the game itself has a page and a setting for them, a trainer tied to each, and a proper switch animation.
q.p: One new page, Version Select, so the choice is not buried in a settings row.
q.m: Settings › Look gets a Version row and a preview that opens the select page. The Main Menu title carries the version tag with a key to change it.
q.k: Very much: Red, Blue, Yellow, Green and Gold versions are how Pokémon games have always been sold, each with a cover Pokémon.

name: Every version gets its own stage
change: Until now the versions shared one layout and changed its paint. This pass gives each one its own staging for the two screens you see most, the title and the pause hub. Blue rises out of a tide under a full moon, with the menu as a staircase of slanted words. Yellow has the trainer climbing out of a TV set, with the menu as a stack of colourful show cards. Green sets the trainer inside an astrolabe ring with the menu running around its rim. Gold deals the menu as seven tarot cards under a spotlight. Each title also shows that version's own cover Pokémon. Red keeps the angled Phantom layout as the baseline. All five versions were checked on every page for cut-off or overlapping text.

q.x: Yes. The five title screens no longer look like recolours of each other; each has its own scene, shapes and movement.
q.b: Passes 6 to 9 changed colours, lettering and panel shapes. This one changes where things stand and how the menu is built, so a version is recognisable even as a silhouette.
q.p: No new pages. Instead the same two pages exist in five different layouts.
q.m: The pause hub is the menu, and it is the page that changes most: a staircase, show cards, a ring, or a card spread. Settings is one of its seven entries in every version.
q.k: Each version has its own cover Pokémon on the title (Charizard, Gyarados, Pikachu, Venusaur, Gengar), the way each Pokémon game has its own box art.
